items.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014
items.q: him and Higgins both had a big influence on me as well as Elvin and a bunch of other guys, Frankie Dunlop, Billy Hart.

ctx.x: Do you ever, when you’re doing those four bar breaks, eight bar breaks or whatever, do you plan ahead for the next break? There was a guy, I read a quote, someone in the Washington Post reviewing, you were playing with someone and it said “wonderfully orchestrated solos.”

No I’m kind of like — because Max was such a big influence on me too. That was my entrance into jazz. So, and him and all those guys, but I mean him and Higgins both had a big influence on me as well as Elvin and a bunch of other guys, Frankie Dunlop, Billy Hart. So when it comes to solos I’m still trying to compose, you know, like Max. I’m trying to say something. So in my solos, if I’ve got a solo I may have some ideas and then I’ll go forthwith, and then from that something else comes. But on the trading,…

I like that word. Conversating. And I have found that the more in tune the rhythm section is the easier it is to play, or the less hard. You’re not feeling like you’re trying to drag people with you or something. It becomes a group effort. So tonight, when you play with — three of the four other guys in the band are in their 70s and 80s. Do you go into that situation thinking I need to change my playing? Or, as opposed to when you might be working with your own quintet?
